info.bio:
Nicolas Rodney Drake (19 de junio de 1948 - 25 de noviembre de 1974) fue un cantautor folk inglés.

Drake publicó sólo tres álbumes en su corta vida - Five Leaves Left (1969), Bryter Layter (1970) y Pink Moon (1972). Five Leaves Left consistía esencialmente en guitarra acústica, con ciertos arreglos orquestales de cuerda y viento, más Bajo y batería. Bryter Layter introdujo un sonido jazz más comercial, con teclados, etc. Pink Moon, grabado en dos sesiones de dos horas a partir de la medianoche

scenes.name: Carreras en solitario: cantautores de finales de los sesenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Los excéntricos de Los Ángeles (David Axelrod, cuyos breakbeats orquestales anticipan el trip-hop; Van Dyke Parks y su música de cámara pop; David Ackles, Kim Fowley, Wild Man Fischer) y los herederos del Greenwich (Laura Nyro, Eric Andersen, David Peel, Angus MacLise y Nico, cuyas letanías fúnebres inventan el rock gótico casi por accidente: Marble Index, Desert Shore). Canadá aporta a Leonard Cohen, Gordon Lightfoot, Joni Mitchell (Blue, Hejira) y Neil Young, que con Dylan y Springsteen forma la gran tríada «moral» de la música americana e inventa la guitarra distorsionada que influirá en el grunge. En Texas, Townes Van Zandt; en Gran Bretaña, Scott Walker, Nick Drake (Pink Moon), Roy Harper, John Martyn, Cat Stevens, Rod Stewart, Eric Burdon y Jack Bruce.

podcast.title: Accidental Overdose Discussion
podcast.body: Matthew Good's personal experience with an accidental overdose prompted a discussion about Nick Drake's death, which is also attributed to an accidental overdose of pills. Conflicting accounts exist, with some suggesting Drake took too many pills at once, while others propose he took a second pill after an initial dose wore off, leading to a fatal combination. "Wasn't this something that Nick Drake had?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Controversial Death Details
podcast.body: The circumstances surrounding Nick Drake's death are subject to differing accounts, even within his family. While some believe he took too many pills accidentally after having a bowl of cereal, others contend he may have taken a pill, fallen asleep, then woken up, had cereal, and taken another pill while disoriented, leading to an accidental overdose. "His family contends, or some of his family contend that he had taken a pill and before and fallen asleep for a brief period or not at all. And they couldn't get back to sleep so he woke up, had a bowl of cereal took another pill because he was out of it from the first one and the combination of the two accidentally killed him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cult Artist Status
podcast.body: During his lifetime, Nick Drake was regarded as a cult artist, with limited commercial success. His work gained significant posthumous recognition, largely propelled by its use in advertising.

podcast.title: Possible Bipolarity
podcast.body: British folk singer Nick Drake is suggested as someone who quite possibly suffered from bipolar disorder, a condition characterized by extreme shifts between manic highs and depressive lows. "British Folk singer Nick Drake, and quite possibly Kurt Cobain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Mortem Praise
podcast.body: Nick Drake is mentioned as an artist who received praise, alongside Jeff Buckley and Elliot Smith, implying a similar post-mortem recognition or heightened appreciation. "Potser Mous Praise for Nick Drake, Jeff Buckley, and Elliot Smith."

podcast.title: Post-VW Ad Sales Boom
podcast.body: Following its debut in a Volkswagen commercial in 2000, sales of Nick Drake's music dramatically increased. Sales went up 500% initially, and then, after the record label added "as featured in the VW ad" stickers to CDs, sales jumped from 6,000 copies a year to 74,000 copies annually in the United States alone.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 2

podcast.title: Record Label Marketing after VW Ad
podcast.body: After witnessing the significant increase in sales following the Volkswagen commercial, Nick Drake's record label responded by adding stickers to his CDs. These stickers read "as featured in the VW ad" to capitalize on the newfound exposure and consumer interest.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Subsequent Licensing of "Pink Moon"
podcast.body: After the success in the Volkswagen commercial, the song "Pink Moon" was subsequently licensed for use in other projects, including various TV shows and movies, generating substantial income.

xref.title: Robert Smith's Early Influences
xref.body: Robert Smith's older siblings introduced him to a diverse range of artists, including The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, Captain Beefheart, David Bowie, Jimi Hendrix, and Nick Drake. The subsequent arrival of punk rock, with bands like Sex Pistols, Ramones, and Elvis Costello, further shaped his musical direction and helped him find his artistic niche. "His older brother and sister had filled his head with beetles and stone songs, but they also subjected him to a lot of Captain B-Fart, and David Bowie, and Jimmy Hendrix and Nick Drake. And then when punk came along, it was Sex Pistols Ramones Elvis Costello. Young Robert found his niche."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Influences
xref.body: Robert Smith's musical upbringing was shaped by his older brother and sister, who introduced him to The Beatles and The Rolling Stones. They also exposed him to more unconventional artists like Captain Beefheart, David Bowie, Jimi Hendrix, and Nick Drake. The arrival of punk further influenced Smith, with bands like the Sex Pistols, Ramones, and Elvis Costello helping him discover his artistic niche. "His older brother and sister had filled his head with beetles and stone songs, but they also subjected him to a lot of Captain B. Fart, and David Bowie, and Jimmy Hendrix and Nick Drake."
